name: Cybersecurity 101
author: Recurse
subject: security
description: Core defensive ideas: the CIA triad, risk, logins and MFA, phishing, SQL injection, XSS and least privilege.

lesson.intro: Security is about protecting information and systems from people who want to misuse them. This lesson covers the vocabulary defenders use, how logins and passwords should work, how attackers trick people, the two web bugs every developer must know (SQL injection and XSS), and the habits that limit damage when something goes wrong.

sections.title: The CIA triad and risk
sections.body:
Security goals are usually described with three words, the CIA triad:

- Confidentiality: only the right people can read the data. Broken by a leaked customer database.
- Integrity: data is not changed without permission. Broken when someone edits a payment amount in transit.
- Availability: the system works when people need it. Broken by a flood of traffic that knocks a site offline.

Three more words describe what can go wrong:

- A threat is someone or something that could cause harm: a criminal group, a careless insider, a flood.
- A vulnerability is a weakness a threat could use: an unpatched server, a weak password, an open storage bucket.
- Risk is how likely harm is and how bad it would be. A useful rule of thumb is risk = likelihood x impact.

A vulnerability with no realistic threat is low risk; the same flaw on an internet-facing server that attackers actively scan for is high risk. Defenders cannot fix everything at once, so they rank work by risk.
sections.tip: An exploit is the actual technique or code that takes advantage of a vulnerability.

check.question: A flood of junk traffic knocks an online shop offline for a day. Which part of the CIA triad was attacked?
choices: Confidentiality
Integrity
Authentication
Availability
check.explanation: Customers could not use the shop, so availability was lost. No data was read (confidentiality) or changed (integrity). Authentication is not part of the CIA triad.

sections.title: Logins: authentication, authorization and passwords
sections.body:
Two checks happen around every login, and mixing them up causes real bugs:

- Authentication (AuthN) answers "who are you?" It verifies identity with a password, a passkey, or a code.
- Authorization (AuthZ) answers "what are you allowed to do?" It runs after login, on every request: can this user see this invoice or open the admin page?

A site should never store passwords in plain text. It stores a one-way hash, and at login it hashes what you typed and compares. Password hashes must be salted and deliberately slow (bcrypt or Argon2), so a stolen database cannot be cracked quickly; the Cryptography Basics pack covers how.

Users have work to do too. Attackers take email and password pairs leaked from one site and try them on others (credential stuffing). A password manager makes it easy to use a long, unique password everywhere.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires proof from two or more different kinds of factor:

- Something you know: a password or PIN.
- Something you have: a phone app code or a hardware security key.
- Something you are: a fingerprint or face scan.

Two items of the same kind, like a password plus a security question, are still one factor. App codes are stronger than SMS codes, and security keys and passkeys are stronger still because they refuse to work on a fake site.
sections.code:
# What the database should hold: a slow, salted hash, never the password
# users table
# username | password_hash
# ana      | $2b$12$6jZ8u922B3FZKNPf/k4aDuhGg5L3QzleGx/Yi0aSxLRCuOj3klf2q

check.question: Which question does authentication answer?
choices: Who are you?
What are you allowed to do?
Is the server online?
Has the data been changed?
check.explanation: Authentication proves identity. Deciding what a known user may do is authorization, a separate check that runs after login.

sections.title: Phishing and social engineering
sections.body:
Social engineering attacks people instead of machines. It is often easier to trick someone into handing over a password than to break the system that stores it.

- Phishing: a fake email or message that gets you to click a link, open an attachment, or type your password into a lookalike site.
- Spear phishing: phishing tailored to one person or team, using real names, projects or invoices to look legitimate.
- Vishing and smishing: the same trick by phone call or text message.
- Pretexting: inventing a believable story ("I am from IT, we are fixing your account") to get information.
- Tailgating: following an employee through a secure door.

Warning signs: urgency or fear ("your account will be closed in 1 hour"), requests for passwords or MFA codes, unexpected attachments, and links whose real domain does not match the sender.

To read a link's real owner, find the part just before the first single slash and read the domain from the right. In `https://example-bank.com.secure-login.net/account`, the registered domain is `secure-login.net`; `example-bank.com` is just a subdomain label the attacker chose.

The defense is a habit: when a message asks for something sensitive, verify through a channel you already trust, such as a known phone number or typing the site address yourself. Legitimate IT staff never need your password or MFA code.
sections.code:
https://login.example-bank.com/account          -> owned by example-bank.com
https://example-bank.com.secure-login.net/      -> owned by secure-login.net
https://example-bank.co/login                   -> owned by example-bank.co (different domain)
sections.tip: Report suspected phishing even if you clicked. Fast reports let the security team block the site before others fall for it.

check.question: Which sign is the strongest hint that an email is phishing?
choices: It greets you by your first name and job title
It arrives late at night, outside normal office hours
It rushes you to log in through a link on an unfamiliar domain
It includes the company logo and a real-looking footer
check.explanation: Pressure to act fast plus a login link on a domain you do not recognize is the classic phishing pattern. Your name and a logo are easy for attackers to copy, so they prove nothing either way.

sections.title: Injection and XSS
sections.body:
Injection happens when user input is glued into code, so the input can change what the code does.

SQL injection: if a program builds a query with string formatting, input like `' OR '1'='1` closes the quote and adds a condition that is always true, returning every row. Worse inputs can read other tables or delete data.

The fix is a parameterized query: the SQL text has placeholders, and the values are sent separately. The database always treats them as data, never as SQL, no matter what characters they contain.

Cross-site scripting (XSS) is injection into HTML. If a page inserts user input into HTML without escaping it, an attacker can submit `<script>...</script>` and their JavaScript runs in other users' browsers, where it can steal session cookies or act as the victim.

- Escape untrusted data for where it goes: `html.escape` turns `<` into `<` so the browser shows it as text.
- Use template engines that escape by default (Jinja2, React) and do not switch it off.
- Add a Content Security Policy and mark session cookies HttpOnly so a missed bug does less damage.

Blocklists that strip words like `script` do not work; attackers have endless other ways to write the same payload.
sections.code:
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
cur = con.cursor()
name = "' OR '1'='1"   # attacker-controlled input

# Vulnerable: input becomes part of the SQL text
cur.execute(f"SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")   # returns every user

# Safe: the value is passed separately from the SQL
cur.execute("SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))   # returns no rows

check.question: Why do parameterized queries stop SQL injection?
choices: They encrypt the input before it reaches the database
The value is sent separately, so it can never change the SQL itself
They strip quote characters and semicolons from the input
They run each query with reduced database permissions
check.explanation: With placeholders, the database parses the SQL first and then binds the value as plain data. No input can add conditions or commands. Removing quotes is a fragile filter, not the reason it works.

sections.title: Least privilege and patching
sections.body:
Assume something will eventually be compromised, and limit how far an attacker can get from there.

Least privilege means every user, program and service gets only the access it needs for its job, and no more.

- A web app's database account can read and write the app's tables, but cannot drop tables or read the HR database.
- Admins use a separate admin account only for admin tasks, and an everyday account for email and browsing.
- Services run as dedicated low-privilege users, not as root or Administrator.
- Access is removed when someone changes role or leaves.

Patching closes known holes. Most breaches use vulnerabilities that already have a fix available; the victim just had not applied it. Public vulnerabilities get CVE identifiers (such as CVE-2021-44228, the Log4Shell bug in Log4j), and attackers start scanning for them within hours or days of disclosure.

- Keep an inventory so you know what software you run.
- Patch internet-facing systems and actively exploited bugs first.
- Turn on automatic updates where you can.

Layering controls like these is called defense in depth: no single control is perfect, so several overlapping ones stop what one misses.
sections.tip: Running something as root "to avoid permission errors" turns any bug in it into full control of the machine.

check.question: A developer runs a web server as root to avoid permission errors. What is the main danger?
choices: The server will run slower because root adds overhead
Root processes write extra logs that fill up the disk
Any exploit of the server hands the attacker the whole machine
Normal users will be unable to log in to the website
check.explanation: A process can do anything its user can do. If a root process is exploited, the attacker inherits root. Under a dedicated low-privilege user, the same bug gives them far less.

keyTerms.definition: The three core security goals: confidentiality, integrity and availability.
How likely a threat is to exploit a vulnerability, combined with how much harm it would cause.
Deciding what an already authenticated user is allowed to do, checked on every request.
Logging in with proof from two or more different kinds of factor: something you know, have, or are.
Manipulating people into giving up information or access, as in phishing, pretexting and tailgating.
An attack where input changes the structure of a database query because it was concatenated into the SQL text.
An attack where unescaped input is placed into a web page, so the attacker's script runs in other users' browsers.
Giving every account and program only the permissions it needs for its job.

summary: Security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability, and defenders rank work by risk: likelihood times impact.
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do, on every request.
Store only slow, salted password hashes, use unique passwords, and turn on MFA, preferably app codes or security keys.
Phishing works on people: check the real domain and verify unexpected requests through a channel you already trust.
Use parameterized queries against SQL injection, escape output against XSS, and limit damage with least privilege and fast patching.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend starting their first office job why they should never share an MFA code, why every account needs its own password, and how to tell that an urgent email asking them to log in is a trap.

questions.question: An attacker on the network secretly changes the amount in a bank transfer from 50 to 5,000 while it is in transit. Which security goal is broken?
choices: Confidentiality
Availability
Integrity
Authorization
questions.explanation: The data was altered without permission, which breaks integrity. Confidentiality would be broken if the attacker only read the transfer, and availability if the transfer could not go through at all.

questions.question: A company's public web server runs software with a known flaw that has not been patched. How should the flaw itself be classified?
choices: A vulnerability
A threat
An exploit
An incident
questions.explanation: An unpatched flaw is a weakness, which makes it a vulnerability. The threat is whoever might use it, the exploit is the technique they would use, and it only becomes an incident once someone actually does.

questions.question: What is the difference between a threat, a vulnerability and a risk?
questions.answer: A threat is someone or something that could cause harm. A vulnerability is a weakness it could use. Risk is how likely it is that the threat exploits the weakness, combined with how bad the damage would be.
questions.explanation: Real risk needs both pieces: a weakness nobody can reach is low risk, and a capable attacker with no weakness to use is also low risk.

questions.question: A logged-in employee opens the payroll page and gets an "access denied" error. Which check stopped them?
choices: Authentication
Encryption
Hashing
Authorization
questions.explanation: The employee is already logged in, so authentication succeeded. The system then decided this user is not allowed to view payroll, which is authorization.

questions.question: What is the three-letter acronym for logging in with two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a code from your phone?
questions.explanation: MFA stands for multi-factor authentication. 2FA, two-factor authentication, is the common case of exactly two factors.

questions.question: Which login combination is true multi-factor authentication?
choices: A password plus the answer to a security question
A password plus a code from an authenticator app
A PIN plus a separate account password
A long password typed twice to confirm it
questions.explanation: A password is something you know and an app on your phone is something you have, so that is two different factors. A password plus a security question or PIN is still only something you know.

questions.question: This sign-up code stores a hash instead of the password. What is the security problem?
questions.code:
import hashlib

def save_user(db, username, password):
    digest = hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest()
    db.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)", (username, digest))
choices: The INSERT statement is open to SQL injection
hexdigest() stores the password in readable form
MD5 is fast and unsalted, so leaked hashes crack quickly
Passwords should be encrypted instead so they can be recovered later
questions.explanation: MD5 is built for speed, so attackers can test billions of guesses per second, and without a salt, identical passwords produce identical hashes. Use a slow, salted password hash such as bcrypt or Argon2. The query is parameterized, so it is safe from injection, and passwords should never be recoverable.

questions.question: Attackers take email and password pairs leaked from one website and try them on banks and email providers. Which habit defeats this attack?
choices: A unique password for every site, stored in a password manager
Adding a new number to the end of your password each year
Clearing your browser cookies and history every day
Only logging in from your home network or work laptop
questions.explanation: This is credential stuffing, and it only works when a password is reused. A unique password per site means one leak unlocks only one account. Tweaking a reused password with a number is easy for attackers to guess.

questions.question: Which link really points to a site owned by example-bank.com?
choices: https://example-bank.com.secure-login.net/account
https://login.example-bank.com/account
https://example-bank-login.com/account
https://secure.example-bank.co/account
questions.explanation: Read the domain from the right, just before the first single slash: login.example-bank.com ends in example-bank.com. The first link is owned by secure-login.net, and the other two are different domains that only look similar.

questions.question: Someone calls claiming to be from IT, says your account is being attacked, and asks you to read out the MFA code you just received. What should you do?
choices: Read the code quickly, since the account is at risk
Give only the first half of the code, to be safe
Ask them for their employee ID, then read the code
Hang up and call IT back on a number you already know
questions.explanation: This is vishing. The code only arrived because the caller is trying to log in as you. Real IT staff never need your MFA code, and an employee ID is easy to fake, so verify through a channel you already trust.

questions.question: What is the name for phishing aimed at one specific person or team, using real details about them to look believable?
questions.explanation: Spear phishing is targeted phishing. Attackers research names, projects and suppliers so the message matches what the victim expects. When the target is a senior executive it is sometimes called whaling.

questions.question: Complete the sqlite3 query so the user's input is passed safely as a parameter.
questions.code:
name = input("Search name: ")
cur.execute("SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE name = _____", (name,))
choices: '{name}'
name
questions.explanation: sqlite3 uses ? as the placeholder and binds the tuple's values to it. A quoted '?' is just the literal text "?", '{name}' is a literal string because there is no f prefix, and a bare name would be read as a column name.

questions.question: A login form builds f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'". An attacker types ' OR '1'='1 as the name. What happens?
choices: The query fails with a syntax error and nothing is returned
The database escapes the quotes automatically
The WHERE clause becomes always true and every user row is returned
Only users literally named ' OR '1'='1 are returned
questions.explanation: The input closes the opening quote and appends OR '1'='1', which is true for every row, so the query returns the whole table. The database cannot escape anything here because the input is already part of the SQL text.

questions.question: This Flask search page works, but a security review flags it. What is the vulnerability?
choices: SQL injection, because q comes from the URL
Reflected XSS, because q goes into the HTML without escaping
The route must use POST instead of GET to be secure
request.args.get crashes if q is missing
questions.explanation: A link like /search?q=<script>...</script> makes the page run the attacker's script in the victim's browser. Escape q (or render a template with auto-escaping). There is no database query, so it is not SQL injection, and the default "" handles a missing q.

questions.question: Complete the function so a user's comment is shown as text instead of being run as HTML.
choices: html.unescape
str.strip
repr
html.escape
questions.explanation: html.escape turns characters like < and > into < and >, so the browser displays them instead of treating them as tags. html.unescape does the opposite and would make the problem worse.

questions.question: A web shop only needs to read products and create orders. Which database account should the app use?
choices: A dedicated account allowed to read products and insert orders
The database admin account, so no query ever fails on permissions
A shared account that every internal app also uses
An account with full rights to the shop's database
questions.explanation: Least privilege: if the app is compromised, the attacker only gets what the app's account can do. With an admin or full-rights account, one SQL injection bug could drop tables or read every other database.

questions.question: A vendor releases a patch for a vulnerability in your internet-facing VPN, and attackers are already exploiting it. What is the best response?
choices: Wait for the next quarterly maintenance window
Apply the patch urgently, ahead of routine updates
Rely on antivirus to catch any attack
Hide the VPN's version number from its login page
questions.explanation: An actively exploited bug on an internet-facing system is the highest priority, because attackers scan for it within hours. Waiting leaves it open, and hiding the version number does not remove the flaw.
